PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR

# Proposition 3
Constitutional Right to Marriage.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Analysis of Measure
#### Background
The federal courts have said that same-sex couples can marry, but outdated language in the California Constitution still says that marriage can only be between a man and a woman.
#### Proposal
Proposition 3 updates the Constitution to match what the federal courts have said about who can marry.
#### Fiscal Effects
Proposition 3 would not change who is allowed to marry in California.
This means there would be no change in revenues or costs to state and local governments.
### Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Language in the California Constitution would be updated to match who currently can marry.
There would be no change in who can marry.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Language in the California Constitution would not be changed.
There would be no change in who can marry.

# November 5, 2024 Ballot Prop. 3
## Proposition 3: Constitutional Right to Marriage. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
### Summary
Proposition 3 is a legislatively referred constitutional amendment.
It would update the language in the California Constitution so that it mirrors what federal courts have ruled about who can marry.
Specifically, the measure repeals Proposition 8 (2008), which defined marriage in the state constitution as between one man and one woman.The proposition would also add text establishing a right to marry as furtherance of the right to life, liberty, the pursuit of happiness, and privacy and the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the state constitution.

PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES

NO

ARGUMENTS
PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

YES

PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.

Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. 2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.

Now I have a good picture of 2026 Prop 3. Let me research more: arguments for and against, economic analysis (e.g., does the tax cause out-migration of high earners?), news coverage from CalMatters, Hoover Institution (opposed perspective), endorsements from newspapers, etc.

Key facts so far:
- Prop 3 (2026) makes permanent the Prop 30 (2012)/Prop 55 (2016) income tax rates on top ~2% of earners (taxable income above ~$371K single / $743K joint), with marginal rates 10.3%, 11.3%, 12.3%; plus the 1% Prop 63 mental health surcharge over $1M → 13.3% top rate, highest in nation.
- Otherwise expires after 2030 (end of 2030 tax year).
- Revenue: $5B–$15B/year depending on economy/stock market.
- Roughly 40% flows to schools/community colleges via Prop 98; rest to other programs including health care; some to rainy day fund.
- Supporters: CTA, CA School Nurses, CA State PTA, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA.
- Opponents: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, CA Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.

Arguments against: California already has highest taxes; volatile revenue source; millionaire out-migration; temporary taxes should stay temporary; Sacramento waste. Also the "permanent" nature removes future voter leverage. There's research (e.g., from Stanford/California Policy Lab) on whether top earners leave due to taxes. Also there was a 2024 study "taxing top incomes" — some research found Prop 30 did cause some increase in out-migration among top earners but modest revenue impact.

PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said.
